about: Patient Pathway – Integrated and Community Care (MBBS0041) is the first of four patient pathways in UCL's Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP) curriculum. It runs alongside the other Year 1 modules across Terms 1 to 3 and continues into Year 2. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue says it aims to help students understand illness from the patient's perspective. Students meet patients, carers and professionals and visit community health and social care services, through some or all of plenaries, tutorials, placements, visits and supervised meetings with patients. The topics follow the catalogue's five learning outcomes, with the last one split in two. The module carries 0 credits; the catalogue does not name its assessment method, but UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 assessment guide says the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests assess across modules, including CPP.
topics: Meeting patients, carers and community health and social care services
Personal histories and social context: illness from the patient's perspective
Your own attitudes, values, beliefs and biases
Inequality, discrimination and access to services

notes.h: Meeting patients, carers and community health and social care services
notes.body:
The first learning outcome of this pathway is to meet patients, carers and health and social care professionals, and to visit community services, to hear how health, illness and support are experienced and delivered. To get the most from those visits you need a working map of how care outside hospital is organised in England.

Who provides care outside hospital
- Primary care: general practice, community pharmacy, dentistry and optometry. General practice is usually the first point of contact and holds the patient's long-term record.
- Community health services: district and community nurses, health visitors, community mental health teams, community rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy), specialist nurses and community palliative care, often working with hospices, most of which are charities.
- Adult social care: help with personal care, home care, day services, equipment and adaptations, and residential or nursing homes. Local authorities assess needs and arrange care, much of which is delivered by private and voluntary providers.
- The voluntary and community sector: charities, faith groups, peer-support groups, food banks and advice services.
- Unpaid carers: family members and friends who provide most day-to-day support for many people with long-term conditions.

A key difference: NHS care is largely free at the point of use, whereas adult social care in England is means-tested, so many people pay towards it. Patients and carers often experience this boundary as confusing.

The Care Act 2014 (England)
- Section 1 places a general duty on local authorities to promote individual wellbeing.
- Section 9 requires a needs assessment for any adult who appears to need care and support; section 10 gives carers the right to a carer's assessment of their own needs.
- Section 42 requires local authorities to make safeguarding enquiries when an adult at risk may be experiencing abuse or neglect.

Integrated care
- Integration means organising services around the person rather than the institution, so that people tell their story once and do not fall through gaps between NHS, social care and voluntary services.
- The Health and Care Act 2022 put integrated care systems on a statutory footing from 1 July 2022. Each has an integrated care board (an NHS body that plans and funds most local NHS services) and an integrated care partnership with local authorities and others. There were 42 at the start; since 2025 many boards have been clustering or merging, so check the current arrangements.
- Primary care networks, introduced in 2019, group neighbouring practices, typically serving about 30,000 to 50,000 patients, and employ extra roles such as clinical pharmacists and social prescribing link workers.
- The government's 10 Year Health Plan for England (Fit for the future, July 2025) describes three shifts: from hospital to community, from analogue to digital, and from sickness to prevention, including neighbourhood health services.

Social prescribing
Link workers connect people to non-medical support such as community groups, exercise, debt advice or arts activities, aiming to address loneliness and social needs. It is widely adopted, but the strength of evidence for its health benefits is still debated.

Why integration matters
Many people live with several long-term conditions at once (multimorbidity). Fragmented care leads to duplicated tests, conflicting advice, delayed hospital discharge and exhaustion for patients and carers. Hearing a patient describe their own journey across services shows this more clearly than any diagram.

Making the most of visits
- Prepare: find out what the service does, who it serves and how people are referred.
- Ask professionals about their role, who they work with and the frustrations of their work, as well as its rewards.
- Notice what the service is like from the user's side: getting there, waiting, information, language and cost.

Exam tips: be ready to name which organisation provides a given service, to distinguish NHS from social care funding, and to explain one benefit and one challenge of integration.

notes.h: Personal histories and social context: illness from the patient's perspective
notes.body:
The pathway's central aim is for you to understand illness from the patient's perspective, and to explore people's personal histories and social context when thinking about their health and social support needs.

Disease, illness and sickness
- Disease: the biomedical abnormality, such as reduced lung function in COPD.
- Illness: the person's own experience of being unwell, including symptoms, fears, meanings and effects on daily life.
- Sickness: the social role and recognition that come with being unwell.
Writers in medical anthropology, notably Arthur Kleinman (The Illness Narratives, 1988), argued that doctors focus on disease while patients live with illness, and that care improves when both are addressed.

The biopsychosocial model
George Engel (Science, 1977) argued that a purely biomedical model cannot explain why the same disease affects people so differently. He proposed that biological, psychological and social factors interact. For a man with COPD, these might be lung damage from smoking (biological), low mood and fear of breathlessness (psychological), and living alone in a flat with stairs on a low income (social). Each affects the others.

Illness narratives
- People make sense of illness through stories. Arthur Frank (The Wounded Storyteller, 1995) described three broad types: restitution (I was ill and will get back to normal), chaos (life feels out of control) and quest (illness becomes a journey that teaches something).
- Listening to the story, rather than interrupting to take a history, shows what matters to the person and builds trust.

Ideas, concerns and expectations (ICE)
A simple way to explore the patient's perspective:
- Ideas: what do you think is causing this?
- Concerns: what worries you most about it?
- Expectations: what were you hoping would happen, or what would help?

The social history
Learn to ask about:
- Home: who lives there, type of housing, stairs, adaptations.
- Daily activities: basic activities of daily living (washing, dressing, eating, toileting, moving about) and wider ones (shopping, cooking, managing money and medicines).
- Support: family, friends, paid carers, community groups; who depends on the patient.
- Work, education and finances.
- Smoking, alcohol and other substances.
- Culture, faith and beliefs that shape how illness and treatment are understood.
- Health literacy: how easily the person can find, understand and use health information.

Person-centred care
- Person-centred care treats people as partners, respecting their values and preferences. A phrase often used is that clinicians should ask "What matters to you?" as well as "What is the matter with you?" (Barry and Edgman-Levitan, 2012).
- Shared decision-making brings together the clinician's knowledge of options and the patient's knowledge of their own life and priorities.

Practical and ethical points on visits
- Introduce yourself as a medical student, explain the purpose of the visit and get the person's agreement; they can decline.
- Keep confidentiality: anonymise anything you write, and do not discuss patients where you could be overheard or on social media.
- Respect boundaries: you are a guest in a person's home or service. Do not give clinical advice beyond your role.
- If something worries you, such as possible abuse or neglect, tell your supervisor promptly.

Exam tips: in scenario questions, show you can move from the disease to the person: identify the biological, psychological and social factors, and say how they change what support the person needs.

Reflection means thinking carefully about an experience so that you learn from it and act differently next time. The pathway asks you to reflect on your professional interactions with patients, carers and professionals, and reflection runs through medical training and a doctor's career.

Why reflect?
- Experience alone does not guarantee learning; reflection turns experience into understanding and better practice.
- It helps you notice your own feelings, assumptions and reactions, which links directly to the pathway's outcome on attitudes and biases.
- It supports wellbeing by giving space to process difficult encounters.

Key thinkers
- Donald Schön (The Reflective Practitioner, 1983) distinguished reflection-in-action (thinking on your feet during an encounter) from reflection-on-action (looking back afterwards).
- David Kolb (1984) described an experiential learning cycle: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation (making sense of it, linking to theory), and active experimentation (trying something new).
- Graham Gibbs (Learning by Doing, 1988) built a six-stage reflective cycle: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan.
- A simple three-question model, associated with Terry Borton (1970) and later John Driscoll: What? So what? Now what?

Using Gibbs' cycle: a worked example
A student visits a day centre and feels awkward when a man with dementia repeats the same question.
- Description: what happened, briefly and factually.
- Feelings: embarrassment, uncertainty, wanting to correct him.
- Evaluation: what went well (staying calm) and badly (rushing the answer).
- Analysis: why? Lack of knowledge about communicating with people with dementia; a belief that repetition needs correcting; observing how staff calmly answered again.
- Conclusion: patience and reassurance matter more than accuracy here; the student's discomfort came from their own expectations.
- Action plan: read guidance on communicating with people living with dementia and practise at the next visit.

Good reflection
- Focus on learning and future action, not a full factual account of the event.
- Be honest about feelings and mistakes; reflection is personal and there is no single correct way to do it.
- Include positive experiences as well as difficult ones.
- Use group reflection (for example tutorials or Balint-style groups) to hear other perspectives.

Professional guidance
- The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, the Conference of Postgraduate Medical Deans, the GMC and the Medical Schools Council jointly published The reflective practitioner: guidance for doctors and medical students (first published 2018). It stresses that reflection is personal, that notes need not record full factual details and should focus on learning, and that group reflection is valuable.
- The GMC states that it does not ask doctors to provide their reflective notes to investigate a concern about them. Reflective notes are not otherwise legally protected, which is one more reason to anonymise them and keep them focused on learning.
- UCL's MBBS requires a portfolio for progression; use your reflections from the pathway to build it, following Year 1 instructions on Moodle.

Confidentiality in reflection
- Remove names, dates of birth, addresses and any detail that could identify a patient, carer or staff member.
- Never discuss identifiable encounters on social media.

Common pitfalls
- Pure description with no analysis.
- Self-criticism with no plan.
- Writing what you think assessors want to hear rather than what you actually learned.

Exam tips: name a model, apply its stages to a specific encounter, and finish with a concrete, realistic action.

notes.h: Your own attitudes, values, beliefs and biases
notes.body:
The pathway asks you to consider how your own attitudes, values, beliefs, perceptions and biases may affect your interactions. Everyone has them; the professional skill is to notice them and stop them harming care.

Definitions
- Values: what you consider important (for example independence, family, honesty).
- Beliefs: what you hold to be true (for example about the causes of illness or the role of doctors).
- Attitudes: your evaluations of people, groups or things, which combine thoughts, feelings and tendencies to act.
- Stereotype: a generalised belief about a group applied to an individual.
- Prejudice: a negative attitude towards a group or its members.
- Discrimination: unfair treatment of people because of their group membership.

Explicit and implicit bias
- Explicit bias is conscious and can be reported.
- Implicit (unconscious) bias refers to automatic associations that can influence judgement without awareness, even in people who hold egalitarian views.
- The Implicit Association Test (Greenwald, McGhee and Schwartz, 1998) measures reaction times to pairings of concepts. It is widely used, but how reliable it is for an individual, and how well its scores predict real behaviour, are debated; treat it as a prompt for reflection rather than a diagnostic test.
- Bias training on its own has mixed evidence of changing behaviour. Changes to systems and routines are generally thought to matter more.

Cognitive biases in clinical thinking
- Anchoring: sticking with a first impression despite new information.
- Confirmation bias: seeking evidence that fits your view and discounting what does not.
- Availability bias: overestimating something because a recent or memorable case comes easily to mind.
- Diagnostic overshadowing: attributing new symptoms to a known condition such as a learning disability or mental illness, so a physical illness is missed. National reviews of deaths of people with learning disabilities in England have repeatedly highlighted this.

How biases show up on the pathway
- Assumptions about who is 'difficult', 'non-compliant' or 'frequent attender'.
- Judgements about lifestyle (smoking, weight, drug use) that reduce empathy.
- Assumptions based on age, accent, appearance, disability or culture, such as assuming an older person cannot use technology, or speaking to a carer instead of the patient.
- Labels in notes, which can follow a patient and shape how future staff treat them.

What helps
- Slow down and notice your first reaction; ask whether it is based on evidence about this person.
- Individuate: focus on the person's own story and circumstances rather than group generalisations.
- Take the other person's perspective deliberately.
- Use neutral, person-first language (a person who uses drugs, rather than a drug user).
- Use structured approaches, such as the same questions for every patient, to reduce variation.
- Seek feedback and reflect afterwards.

Professional standards
- The GMC's Good medical practice (in effect from 30 January 2024) requires doctors to treat patients fairly and respect their dignity, not to unfairly discriminate, and to act on discriminatory behaviour they witness. The GMC's guidance for medical students, Achieving good medical practice, applies the same expectations to students.
- Your personal beliefs must not affect patients' care in ways that disadvantage them; GMC guidance on personal beliefs explains the limits.
- Personal values still matter: they underpin compassion and integrity, as long as patients' own values and choices are respected.

Exam tips: in scenario questions, name the specific bias, explain how it could change care, and give a concrete step that reduces its effect.

The final learning outcome asks you to consider how diversity, vulnerability, stigma, inequality and discrimination affect people's lives and their access to services. This note covers diversity, vulnerability and stigma; the next covers inequality, discrimination and access.

Diversity
- Diversity means the many ways people differ: age, disability, ethnicity, culture, language, faith, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, social class, education and more.
- In Great Britain the Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.
- Intersectionality, a term introduced by Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989), describes how several characteristics combine to shape a person's experience; an older disabled woman from a minority ethnic group may face barriers that no single category explains.
- Valuing diversity in care means not assuming, asking people about their needs and preferences, and adapting services rather than expecting everyone to fit one model.

Vulnerability
- Vulnerability is not a fixed trait of a person; it arises from circumstances that increase the risk of harm or reduce the ability to protect oneself or to get help. Examples include serious illness, disability, frailty, cognitive impairment, homelessness, poverty, insecure immigration status, language barriers, abusive relationships and social isolation.
- Labelling whole groups as 'vulnerable' can be disempowering; focus on what makes this person vulnerable in this situation and what support they want.
- Under the Care Act 2014 (section 42), the local authority must make safeguarding enquiries when an adult has needs for care and support, is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and because of those needs cannot protect themselves.
- The statutory guidance sets out six safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability.
- As a student, if you are concerned that someone is at risk, tell your supervisor or the professional responsible promptly; do not investigate yourself.

Stigma
- Erving Goffman (Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity, 1963) described stigma as an attribute that discredits a person in the eyes of others. He distinguished the discredited (whose difference is visible or known) from the discreditable (whose difference could be revealed, so they must manage information about themselves).
- Graham Scambler and Anthony Hopkins (1986), studying epilepsy, distinguished enacted stigma (actual discrimination) from felt stigma (shame and fear of discrimination). They found felt stigma could be more disruptive than enacted stigma.
- Bruce Link and Jo Phelan (2001) described stigma as labelling, stereotyping, separation ('us and them'), status loss and discrimination, occurring where there are differences in power.
- Internalised (self-) stigma happens when people accept negative stereotypes about themselves, damaging self-esteem and help-seeking.

Conditions commonly stigmatised include mental illness, HIV and other infections, obesity, substance use, homelessness, some disabilities and some skin conditions.

Effects of stigma on health and care
- Delayed help-seeking and disclosure.
- Poorer care when professionals hold negative attitudes, including diagnostic overshadowing.
- Social isolation, unemployment and loss of housing.
- Stress, which can itself worsen health.

What clinicians and students can do
- Use respectful, person-first language and avoid labels in notes.
- Ask about and respect how people describe themselves.
- Challenge stigmatising comments by colleagues appropriately, and reflect on your own reactions.
- Involve people with lived experience in teaching and service design.

Exam tips: use Goffman, Scambler and Hopkins, or Link and Phelan to analyse a case, and always connect stigma to a concrete effect on access to care.

notes.h: Inequality, discrimination and access to services
notes.body:
Health is not shared equally. The pathway asks you to see how inequality and discrimination shape people's lives and their access to services, often more powerfully than any single treatment.

Key definitions
- Health inequalities: unfair and avoidable differences in health between groups of people. Margaret Whitehead's influential definition of inequity (around 1990) stresses differences that are unnecessary, avoidable, unfair and unjust.
- They occur across socio-economic groups, between areas, between groups with protected characteristics, and for socially excluded groups.

The social gradient
- Health tends to improve step by step with social position, not only at the very bottom. The Marmot Review, Fair Society, Healthy Lives (2010), and its follow-up, Health Equity in England: The Marmot Review 10 Years On (2020), described this gradient and called for action across the whole of society.
- Dahlgren and Whitehead's 'rainbow' model (1991) places the individual at the centre, surrounded by layers of influence: individual lifestyle factors; social and community networks; living and working conditions (such as housing, work, education, healthcare); and wider socio-economic, cultural and environmental conditions.
- Office for National Statistics data for England, 2022 to 2024 (published April 2026, using deprivation deciles of the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025): the estimated gap in life expectancy at birth between the most and least deprived areas (the slope index of inequality) was 10.4 years for males and 8.0 years for females, and the gap in healthy life expectancy was 19.3 years for males and 20.1 years for females. These figures are as at the time of writing (October 2026); check the ONS for any newer release.

The inverse care law
Julian Tudor Hart (The Lancet, 1971) wrote that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served. More deprived areas often have greater need but fewer resources per head of need.

Barriers to access
- Practical: cost of travel, time off work, opening hours, distance, digital-only booking.
- Communication: language, literacy, sensory impairment, learning disability.
- Organisational: complex systems, short appointments, documentation demands.
- Personal and social: past bad experiences, mistrust, stigma, fear of charges or immigration checks.

Some UK rules and initiatives to know
- GP registration in England: there is no contractual duty to ask for proof of identity, address or immigration status, and practices should not refuse registration because a person cannot provide them (BMA guidance, 2024). People experiencing homelessness can register using a temporary address (such as a day centre) or the practice's own address.
- Interpreting: NHS England guidance advises using professional interpreters and not relying on family and friends, especially children.
- The Accessible Information Standard (since 2016) requires NHS and publicly funded adult social care services to identify, record, flag, share and meet the communication needs of people with a disability, impairment or sensory loss.
- NHS England's Core20PLUS5 approach focuses on the most deprived 20% of the population, plus locally identified groups, and five clinical areas for adults (with a separate version for children and young people).
- Inclusion health groups are socially excluded people who often face very poor health, including people experiencing homelessness, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities, vulnerable migrants, sex workers, people with drug and alcohol dependence, and people in contact with the justice system.

Discrimination and the law (Equality Act 2010)
- Direct discrimination (section 13): treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic.
- Indirect discrimination (section 19): a rule or practice applied to everyone that puts a protected group at a particular disadvantage without justification.
- Failure to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people (sections 20 and 21).
- Harassment (section 26) and victimisation (section 27).
- The public sector equality duty (section 149) requires public bodies, including the NHS, to have due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations.

What doctors and students can do
- Ask about social circumstances and barriers routinely, not only when someone looks disadvantaged.
- Make reasonable adjustments, such as longer appointments, easy-read information or a quiet waiting area.
- Signpost to advice and community support, and record communication needs.
- Speak up about discriminatory practice and support quality improvement aimed at reducing inequalities.

Exam tips: use the correct term (inequality vs inequity; direct vs indirect discrimination), cite one framework or dataset accurately, and always link the inequality to a specific barrier and a practical response.

questions.q: An 82-year-old woman with heart failure needs help with washing and dressing at home after discharge. Which organisation is responsible for assessing her for this personal care in England?
options: The integrated care board's continuing healthcare team in every case
The local authority adult social care service
questions.why: Help with personal care such as washing and dressing is social care, and under the Care Act 2014 the local authority must assess anyone who appears to need care and support. Her GP coordinates medical care and may refer her, but does not assess or arrange personal care. NHS continuing healthcare applies only when someone's needs are primarily health needs and they meet specific eligibility criteria, so it is not the default route. Charities may provide support, but the statutory duty to assess lies with the local authority.

questions.q: What do primary care networks in England employ social prescribing link workers to do?
options: Carry out Care Act needs assessments
Connect people to non-medical community support for their social needs
questions.why: Link workers help people find community activities, groups and advice services to address loneliness, money worries and other social needs. The word 'prescribing' tempts people to think they prescribe drugs, but they do not. Care Act needs assessments are a local authority duty. Booking outpatient appointments is an administrative function of hospitals and practices, not the role of link workers.

questions.q: Explain what 'integrated care' means and give two benefits and one challenge of integrating health and social care.
markScheme: Definition: care organised around the person, coordinated across NHS, social care and voluntary sectors
Benefit: fewer gaps or duplication; people tell their story once
Benefit: smoother discharge and more care at home or in the community
Challenge: different funding and charging (free NHS vs means-tested social care), organisations, IT systems or workforce pressures
questions.modelAnswer: Integrated care means organising care around the person, so that NHS, social care and voluntary services work together rather than as separate organisations. One benefit is less duplication and fewer gaps: the patient tells their story once and services share plans. A second benefit is that coordinated community support can prevent avoidable admissions and allow quicker discharge home. A challenge is that the sectors are funded and run differently: NHS care is free at the point of use but adult social care is means-tested and arranged by local authorities, and organisations often use separate records and face their own workforce pressures.

questions.q: During a home visit, a woman with COPD says she stopped going to her pulmonary rehabilitation class because the bus fare is too expensive. In a biopsychosocial analysis, which domain does this barrier belong to?
questions.why: Cost of transport is a social and economic factor, part of the social domain. The biological domain covers her lung disease and its physical effects; breathlessness might be another barrier, but it is not the one she describes. The psychological domain covers mood, beliefs and coping, such as fear of breathlessness. Pharmacological is not a domain of Engel's model; medicines would sit within the biological domain.

questions.q: A student asks a patient, 'What do you think is causing your symptoms?' Which part of the ICE framework is this?
questions.why: Asking what the patient thinks is causing the problem explores their Ideas. Concerns would be what worries them most, for example 'Is there anything you are worried this might be?'. Expectations would be what they hope will happen or what they want from the consultation. Examination is not part of ICE; the E stands for Expectations.

questions.q: Using the biopsychosocial model, analyse how a long-term condition might affect a 70-year-old man with COPD who lives alone.
markScheme: Biological: breathlessness, reduced exercise tolerance, exacerbations, other conditions
Psychological: anxiety about breathlessness, low mood, loss of confidence, beliefs about illness
Social: living alone, isolation, stairs or housing, income, ability to shop or attend appointments
Interaction: e.g. anxiety worsens breathlessness, isolation worsens mood and reduces activity
Implication: support needs span health, social care and community services
questions.modelAnswer: Biologically, COPD causes breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance, with exacerbations that may lead to admissions; he may also have other conditions such as heart disease. Psychologically, fear of breathlessness can cause anxiety and avoidance of activity, and loss of independence may lower his mood and confidence. Socially, living alone may mean isolation, difficulty shopping or managing stairs, and problems getting to appointments, especially on a low income. These interact: anxiety makes breathlessness feel worse, avoiding activity leads to further deconditioning, and isolation deepens low mood. His needs therefore span medical treatment, pulmonary rehabilitation, psychological support and social care or community help.

questions.q: In Gibbs' reflective cycle, at which stage would you link your experience to wider knowledge or theory to explain why things happened as they did?
questions.why: Analysis is where you make sense of the situation, drawing on knowledge, theory and others' perspectives to explain what happened. Description is only the factual account of the event. Feelings records your emotions at the time, such as anxiety or embarrassment. The action plan comes last and states what you will do differently, once analysis and conclusion are complete.

questions.q: A student, while talking to a patient, notices the patient becoming upset and changes her approach on the spot. In Schön's terms, what is this?
questions.why: Adjusting your approach during the encounter is reflection-in-action. Reflection-on-action happens afterwards, when you look back on the event. Abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation are stages of Kolb's cycle, not Schön's distinction; active experimentation means trying out a new approach in a later experience after reflecting, not adapting in the moment.

questions.q: State four features of good reflective practice for a medical student, according to current UK guidance and good practice.
markScheme: Focuses on learning and future action rather than a full factual record
Honest and personal; no single right way; includes feelings
Covers positive as well as negative experiences; group reflection is valuable
Anonymised to protect confidentiality; leads to a specific, realistic action plan
questions.modelAnswer: Good reflection focuses on what you learned and what you will do next, rather than recording every factual detail of the event. It is honest and personal: there is no single correct way to reflect, and it is fine to explore your feelings and mistakes. It includes positive experiences as well as difficult ones, and group reflection with peers or tutors brings out other perspectives. Finally, it must be anonymised so that no patient, carer or colleague can be identified, and it should end with a specific, realistic action plan.

questions.q: A man with a learning disability who usually shouts when distressed is shouting more than usual. Staff assume this is 'his behaviour', and a painful dental abscess is missed for a week. Which bias best describes this?
questions.why: Attributing a new change to a known condition (here his learning disability and usual behaviour) so that a physical cause is missed is diagnostic overshadowing. Availability bias would involve over-weighting a recent memorable case. Confirmation bias, seeking evidence that supports a view already held, may contribute, but the specific error of explaining new symptoms by an existing diagnosis has its own name. The halo effect is letting one positive trait colour overall judgement, which does not fit.

questions.q: Which statement about the Implicit Association Test is most accurate?
options: It reliably diagnoses whether an individual will discriminate against patients
It measures automatic associations, but its predictive value for individual behaviour is debated
It measures explicit, consciously reported attitudes
It has been withdrawn because it measures nothing
questions.why: The test uses reaction times to detect automatic associations between concepts, and researchers still debate how reliable it is for individuals and how well scores predict behaviour. Claiming it reliably diagnoses discriminatory behaviour overstates the evidence. It is designed to measure implicit, not explicit, attitudes; explicit attitudes are measured by asking people directly. It has not been withdrawn, and the debate is about how much it predicts, not about it measuring nothing.

questions.q: A student notices she feels irritated with a patient who continues to smoke despite severe COPD. Explain how this attitude could affect care and describe two ways she could manage it.
markScheme: Recognises the judgement as an attitude or bias (blame for 'lifestyle' illness)
Effect: less empathy, less time or information, patient feels judged, worse engagement or disclosure
Strategy: reflect on the reaction; understand nicotine addiction and the social context of smoking
Strategy: non-judgemental, person-centred approach (ICE, person-first language), focus on what matters to the patient
questions.modelAnswer: Her irritation reflects a judgement that the patient is to blame for his illness. If unchecked it could reduce her empathy, make her spend less time explaining things or listening, and leave the patient feeling judged, so he may disclose less or disengage from care. First, she can reflect on the reaction and learn about nicotine addiction and the social and psychological reasons people keep smoking, which reframes it as a health problem rather than a moral failing. Second, she can use a non-judgemental, person-centred approach: explore his ideas, concerns and expectations, use neutral language and focus on what matters to him, offering support to stop smoking without blame.

questions.q: A man with well-controlled epilepsy has never been discriminated against, but avoids telling employers and friends because he fears rejection. According to Scambler and Hopkins, what is this?
questions.why: Fear and shame about possible discrimination, leading him to conceal his condition, is felt stigma. Enacted stigma would mean actual episodes of discrimination, which he has not experienced. Diagnostic overshadowing is a clinical reasoning error, not a person's experience of stigma. Indirect discrimination is a legal concept under the Equality Act about policies that disadvantage a protected group, not his personal fear.

questions.q: Under section 42 of the Care Act 2014, which of these is NOT one of the conditions for a local authority safeguarding enquiry?
options: The adult is experiencing, or is at risk of, abuse or neglect
Because of those needs, the adult cannot protect themselves
The adult has needs for care and support
questions.why: Lack of mental capacity is not a requirement: people with capacity can still be adults at risk, although their wishes carry great weight in deciding what happens. The other three statements are exactly the three conditions in section 42: care and support needs, experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and inability to protect themselves as a result of those needs.

questions.q: Using a named model of stigma, explain how stigma might reduce access to healthcare for a person with severe mental illness.
markScheme: Names and describes a model (e.g. Goffman; Scambler and Hopkins enacted vs felt; Link and Phelan components)
Felt or internalised stigma: shame and fear lead to delayed help-seeking or non-disclosure
Enacted stigma by professionals: negative attitudes, being dismissed
Diagnostic overshadowing: physical symptoms attributed to mental illness
Wider effects: isolation, unemployment, housing problems that further limit access
questions.modelAnswer: Link and Phelan describe stigma as labelling, stereotyping, separation, status loss and discrimination occurring where there is a difference in power. A person labelled with severe mental illness may be stereotyped as dangerous or unreliable and treated as 'other'. Internalised and felt stigma can make them ashamed and fearful of being judged, so they delay seeking help or do not disclose symptoms. Enacted stigma from professionals, such as being dismissed or not believed, discourages return visits. Diagnostic overshadowing may lead clinicians to attribute physical symptoms to the mental illness, so conditions such as heart disease are missed. Status loss through unemployment, isolation and housing problems further limits access to services.

questions.q: A GP practice requires all new patients to show a utility bill in their own name before registering. This disproportionately excludes people experiencing homelessness and some migrants. Which concept best describes this?
options: Indirect discrimination or an unjustified access barrier
questions.why: A rule applied to everyone that puts particular groups at a disadvantage is the pattern of indirect discrimination where a protected characteristic such as race is involved, and in any case it is an unjustified barrier: practices have no contractual duty to demand proof of address and should not refuse registration without it. Direct discrimination would mean treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic itself, such as refusing a patient because of their race. The inverse care law describes a population-level mismatch between need and care, not a specific practice rule. Positive action means lawful steps to help disadvantaged groups, the opposite of this.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the social gradient in health identified in the Marmot Review (2010)?
options: Only the poorest 10% have worse health; everyone else has similar health
Health inequalities are explained entirely by differences in smoking
Wealthier people have worse health because of stress
Health improves step by step with each rise in social position
questions.why: Marmot showed a gradient: at each step up the social scale, health is better, so it is not only the poorest who are affected. The idea that only the poorest tenth do worse misses this gradient and is the common misconception the review set out to correct. Smoking contributes to inequalities, but the review emphasised the wider social determinants, such as early childhood, education, work and income, so 'entirely' is wrong. The data show the opposite of the claim that wealthier people have worse health.

questions.q: A refugee who speaks little English struggles to get care for her child's asthma. Identify barriers she may face and suggest how services should respond.
markScheme: Language and communication barrier; need for professional interpreter (not family, especially not children)
Uncertainty about entitlement or fear of charges or immigration checks; GP registration does not require ID or address
Practical barriers: cost of travel, digital booking, unfamiliarity with the system
Social factors: housing (damp, overcrowding), poverty, isolation, trauma or mistrust
Response: register with GP, professional interpreter, translated or accessible information, longer appointments, signpost to support organisations
questions.modelAnswer: She faces a language barrier: she may not be able to describe symptoms or understand treatment plans, so services should book a professional interpreter rather than relying on her child to interpret. She may be unsure of her entitlements or fear charges or immigration checks; she should be told she can register with a GP without proof of identity, address or immigration status. Practical barriers include travel costs, digital-only booking and unfamiliarity with how the NHS works. Social factors such as damp or overcrowded housing can worsen asthma, and past trauma may cause mistrust. Services should register her, use interpreters, give accessible and translated information, offer longer appointments, and signpost to refugee support and housing advice.

questions.q: Mr K is a 74-year-old widower with COPD and heart failure who lives alone in a third-floor flat. He has had three hospital admissions this year. Using the biopsychosocial model and your knowledge of community health and social care in England, discuss the factors affecting his health and how integrated care could support him.
markScheme: Biological: COPD, heart failure, multimorbidity, exacerbations, frailty
Psychological: anxiety about breathlessness, low mood, loneliness after bereavement, loss of confidence
Social: living alone, stairs, isolation, income, ability to shop or cook, carers or lack of them
Patient perspective: exploring his ideas, concerns, expectations and what matters to him
Services: GP and PCN roles, community nursing, pulmonary/cardiac rehabilitation, social care needs assessment (Care Act 2014), voluntary sector, social prescribing
Integration: shared care plan, MDT, ICB/ICS context, reducing admissions and duplication
Challenges: funding boundaries (means-tested social care), workforce, information sharing; inequality and access
Clear structure and balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr K's three admissions suggest that his care is not meeting his needs, and the biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) helps explain why.

Biologically, he has two long-term conditions that interact: COPD and heart failure both cause breathlessness and reduced exercise tolerance, and an exacerbation of one can tip the other into decompensation. Multimorbidity often brings several medicines and appointments, and he may be becoming frail.

Psychologically, breathlessness is frightening, and anxiety can worsen it, leading him to avoid activity and lose fitness. Being widowed and living alone raises his risk of loneliness and depression, which can reduce motivation to manage his conditions and make him more likely to call for help in a crisis.

Socially, a third-floor flat may trap him if there is no lift, making it hard to shop, attend appointments or go to rehabilitation. His income, whether he can cook and whether anyone checks on him all matter. Without support, small problems such as running out of food or medicines can lead to admission.

Understanding his own perspective is essential: exploring his ideas, concerns and expectations, and asking what matters to him, might reveal, for example, that he most wants to stay at home, or that he fears dying alone.

Integrated care could help in several ways. His GP practice and primary care network can coordinate a single care plan and review his medicines. Community nurses and specialist heart failure or respiratory nurses can monitor him at home and act early on deterioration. Pulmonary and cardiac rehabilitation improve exercise capacity and confidence. Under the Care Act 2014 the local authority should assess his care and support needs, which might lead to home care, equipment or help with moving to more suitable housing. A social prescribing link worker could connect him to community groups to reduce loneliness, and voluntary organisations can offer befriending or practical help. A multidisciplinary team meeting bringing these together, under integrated care board arrangements created by the Health and Care Act 2022, should share information so he tells his story once.

There are challenges. NHS care is free but social care is means-tested, which may deter him from accepting help. Services face workforce pressures, and records are not always shared. If he lives in a deprived area, the inverse care law suggests services may be stretched exactly where need is greatest.

In conclusion, Mr K's admissions reflect the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors, not just his lung and heart disease. A person-centred, integrated approach that combines medical management with social care, rehabilitation and community support offers the best chance of keeping him well and at home, in line with the national shift from hospital to community care.

questions.q: 'Reflection turns experience into learning.' Using a recognised model, show how a medical student could reflect on an encounter during a community visit in which they became aware of their own bias, and discuss the benefits and limits of reflective practice.
markScheme: Names and accurately describes a model (e.g. Gibbs 1988, Kolb 1984, Schön 1983, What/So what/Now what)
Applies each stage to a specific, plausible encounter involving bias
Identifies the bias accurately (e.g. stereotype, anchoring, diagnostic overshadowing) and its possible effect on care
Concrete, realistic action plan
Benefits: learning, insight into attitudes, wellbeing, patient care; group reflection
Limits: can become descriptive or performative; written for assessors; time; legal or confidentiality issues (anonymise; GMC does not ask for reflective notes in investigations)
Refers to current guidance (The reflective practitioner, joint guidance 2018)
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Reflection means deliberately examining an experience to learn from it. Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988) provides a structure with six stages, which can be applied to an encounter on the Integrated and Community Care pathway.

Description: on a visit to a drug and alcohol recovery service, a student met a woman in her thirties who described her recovery from heroin dependence. Before the visit the student had expected service users to be unreliable and had planned only brief questions.

Feelings: the student felt nervous beforehand and later uncomfortable, realising that the woman was articulate, organised and caring for two children, which contradicted the student's expectations.

Evaluation: the student listened well once the conversation started, but at first asked closed questions and avoided eye contact, which the woman may have noticed.

Analysis: the student's expectations reflected a stereotype about people who use drugs, probably absorbed from media portrayals. Link and Phelan's account of stigma, with labelling, stereotyping and separation, helps explain this. If carried into practice, the bias could lead to less empathy, shorter consultations and missed physical problems, a form of diagnostic overshadowing. The woman described exactly this experience in an emergency department, where her pain had been dismissed as drug-seeking.

Conclusion: the student recognised that the bias was the student's own, and that respectful, person-first language and genuine curiosity about people's stories are essential.

Action plan: the student will read about the experiences of people who use drugs in healthcare, use person-first language in notes and conversation, and at the next visit start with open questions and notice first reactions, discussing them at the next tutorial.

Benefits of reflection include turning experience into lasting learning, making unconscious attitudes visible, supporting wellbeing after difficult encounters and ultimately improving patient care. The joint guidance The reflective practitioner (AoMRC, COPMeD, GMC and Medical Schools Council, 2018) stresses that reflection is personal, should focus on learning rather than a full factual record, and benefits from group discussion, where peers can challenge assumptions.

There are limits. Reflection can become purely descriptive, or performative when students write what they think assessors want. It takes time, and insight into one's own biases is limited by those very biases, which is why feedback from others matters. There are confidentiality concerns: notes must be anonymised, and although the GMC says it does not ask doctors for their reflective notes to investigate concerns, notes are not otherwise legally protected. Finally, individual reflection cannot fix structural problems such as stigma built into services.

In conclusion, structured reflection does turn experience into learning, but only when it is honest, analytical and followed by action, and when it is supported by feedback and by changes to the systems in which care is delivered.
